title: Security & governance — where it stands
eyebrow: Capability positioning · read from the source, not from memory
thesis: Most security stacks are a bag of primitives; Softanza's is a doctrine. One capability lattice — `effectful · sensing · compute · inference` — and three postures gate every dangerous act uniformly, so an LLM actor (holding `inference` only) is refused a secret, a file write or a deployment by construction, not by a rule someone remembered to write. On top sit a full identity stack (OIDC, SAML, WebAuthn — both sides) and an engine-computed tamper-evident audit ledger. The gaps are a unified injection-defense surface and the still-unbuilt plugin governance — and there is no formal threat-model document yet.
grid_title: Twelve lanes, each against its category leader
grid_lede: Every lane names what actually ships, the tools it is fair to measure against, and the one thing still owed. Ratings are earned by what the guards prove — and security is unusually well-guarded: roughly 530 core, 417 identity and 88 governance assertions, though they live under `test/system`, `test/cluster` and `test/governance`, not a `test/security` dir.

lanes.engine: One capability lattice (`effectful/sensing/compute/inference`) and three postures (`trusted/external/sandboxed`) enforce six checkpoints: file commit, secret reveal, secret store, deployment, platform deploy, and `StzCheckNoLLMEffectful`. Agents rehearse in a `stzVirtualFileSystem` twin; only a committing actor runs the `stzUpdatePlan` under three gates.
lanes.owed: A genuinely novel, coherent model no mainstream library ships — the LLM actor's lack of `effectful` is the single fact every gate rests on. The remaining reach is extending it to plugins (lane 12).

lanes.engine: A full modern stack: `stzAuth` (sessions-as-tokens, TTL, constant-time), TOTP 2FA, WebAuthn passkeys, OIDC client and provider, SAML SP and IdP, and HMAC request signing with a freshness window + nonce replay cache. All crypto verbs engine-backed; ~417 guarded assertions.
lanes.owed: Password-reset-through-the-store is named as remaining; and being an IdP is protocol-complete but has no admin console or federation breadth — it is a library, not Keycloak the product.

lanes.engine: `stzSecurityLedger` over `engine/src/seclog.zig`: a bounded, hash-chained ring whose digest is computed in-engine, so a caller cannot forge it. Seal-to-file, verify (a broken link is named), rich pivots (by actor/subject/kind/trace/outcome), and `stzSecurityAttestation` for custody.
lanes.owed: The guarantee is honestly scoped — it detects retroactive edits on exported evidence, not an attacker already running in-process (who can wipe the ring). That limit is stated in the doc and matched by the guards.

lanes.engine: "Engine-backed, never hand-rolled": `crypto.zig` ships SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256, PBKDF2 (100k rounds), constant-time compare, CSPRNG, TOTP, ES256/RS256 sign+verify+keypair, b64url; RSA and X.509 go through vendored mbedTLS — a vetted library, not new code.
lanes.owed: A curated subset: no authenticated symmetric encryption (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305) for data-at-rest, and only PBKDF2 among password KDFs (no Argon2/scrypt). Hashing, signing and KDF are covered; sealing is not.

lanes.engine: `stzSecretStore` is the one governed door: register / rotate / revoke, and every `Reveal(name, actor)` is gated and audited (a refusal emits a security event). Secrets self-redact — config serializes a `Descriptor()`, never a value — with lazy env/file/vault sources.
lanes.owed: The redaction and governed-reveal defaults are arguably ahead of Vault's, but no real backend adapter ships (proven only against the in-memory `stzVaultResolver`), and there is no scheduled rotation.

lanes.engine: `stzSecurityGraph` models the security surface as actors/tools/secrets/edges and answers `ReachesEffectful`, `BlastRadius(secret)` and `PathExists` — catching multi-hop escalation a flag check misses. `stzSecurityRule` is-a graph rule and feeds the one CI gate (`stzRuleReport`) alongside code, agent and org domains.
lanes.owed: The reachability architecture is distinctive, but only three security rules ship (two ERROR, one WARN) — a thin catalogue next to OPA's or semgrep's ecosystems. The seam is ready for many more.

lanes.engine: `stzSecurityEvent` is a typed record over a closed kind-catalog, carrying a MITRE ATT&CK technique field and an OCSF JSON export for SIEM interop. The redaction law is enforced at construction — an event records a descriptor, never a value — so telemetry cannot leak a secret.
lanes.owed: Redaction is strong, but there is no PII detection / classification / DLP surface — the law protects known secrets, not free-text data it has never been told about.

lanes.engine: A full runtime chain: `stzDetection` (burst / sequence / any, with a corroboration law) → `stzSecuritySentinel` (edge-triggered) → `stzIncident` (timeline, path, blast radius) → `stzResponsePlan` (containment as a governed act — an LLM's `MayCommit` is false) → `stzSecurityDrill` (adversary emulation vs a real spawned app).
lanes.owed: Only three detection shapes ship (stated to cover the common patterns); no anomaly/ML detection and no Sigma-rule interop for the wider detection ecosystem.

lanes.engine: `stzSecurityAttestation` makes a custody statement over a sealed ledger, and evidence crosses process boundaries as a sealed + attested file (the drill's findings, an incident's proof). Export is treated as a `sensing` act — an LLM may analyze evidence, it may not export it.
lanes.owed: Custody is internal (self-signed over the ledger hash); interop with an external attestation ecosystem (in-toto layouts, transparency logs) is not yet a story.

lanes.engine: mTLS and TLS ride vendored mbedTLS, with a smoke guard (`test/cluster/mtls_narrated.ring`) and engine `fuzz_tls.zig`. Certificate helpers (key, SHA-256 fingerprint, info, readability) live in the security module.
lanes.owed: Transport lives in the cluster / reactive / appserver planes, not security, and is shallow: no cert-lifecycle management, OCSP or cipher-policy governance. It works; it is not a managed TLS surface.

lanes.engine: The primitives exist, scattered: HTML/URL escaping in `encode.zig`, the XML parser closing XXE by construction, request signing against forgery. Real defenses, in the right places.
lanes.owed: No unified injection-defense surface in security: no central validation/sanitization governance, no SQLi / command-injection / path-traversal helpers, no CSRF/XSS toolkit. The OWASP-shaped lane is distributed, not owned.

lanes.engine: A designed doctrine — "a plugin is a governed foreign capability" — that would extend the capability lattice to third-party code (`SOFTANZA_PLUGIN_PLAN.md` + a comparative study).
lanes.owed: Design docs and a recovered archive only — `base/plugin/` is not loaded in `stzBase.ring`. The seam that would make foreign code safe is planned, not shipped (this lane's full rating is the Extensibility group's page).

gaps_title: The gaps, ordered by return — not by size
gaps_lede: Three tiers. The first closes an OWASP-shaped hole and a data-at-rest one; the second is cheap and buys trust; the third is strategic. Value is impact on the library's security posture; effort is a rough engineering read.

items.title: A unified injection-defense surface
items.text: Central validation / sanitization governance covering XSS, SQLi, command injection and path traversal — the OWASP Top-10 core. The escaping primitives already ship; what is missing is one owned surface that a caller reaches for and the CI gate can check.

items.title: Authenticated symmetric encryption + a modern KDF
items.text: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for data-at-rest, and Argon2 alongside PBKDF2. The secret store governs access but cannot seal a value at rest without an AEAD — the one crypto gap that limits the keyring.

tiers.title: Tier B — cheap and high-leverage (mostly trust)

items.title: A formal threat model, mapped to guards
items.text: The module makes honestly-scoped guarantees (the ledger doc names its in-process limit), but there is no STRIDE/threat-model document. Writing one — each guarantee → the assertion that proves it — turns implicit trust into an auditable claim.

items.title: A shipped Vault / KMS backend adapter
items.text: The `stzVaultResolver` seam is proven only against the in-memory reference. One real adapter (HashiCorp Vault or a cloud manager) turns the keyring from a reference design into a deployable one.

items.title: Scheduled rotation + password reset
items.text: Both are named as remaining: automatic secret rotation on a schedule, and password-reset flowing through the store. Small additions to surfaces (`RotateQ`, `stzAuth`) that already exist.

items.title: Ship plugin / foreign-capability governance
items.text: Wire the designed plugin doctrine into the capability lattice and the CI gate, so third-party code becomes governed capability rather than trust. The distinctive safe-world model's natural next frontier.

items.title: Grow the security-rule catalogue
items.text: Three rules today. The reachability seam is built to carry many — a real catalogue (misconfig, over-privilege, exposure patterns) feeding the one CI gate would make it a live policy engine against OPA/semgrep, not a demonstrator.

items.title: Anomaly detection + DLP
items.text: Beyond the three fixed detection shapes: statistical/anomaly detection over the ledger, Sigma-rule interop, and a PII-classification / DLP layer so redaction protects data it was never explicitly handed.

notes.lead: The honesty line on the ratings.
notes.text: Security is heavily guarded — roughly a thousand assertions across the identity, ledger, detection, reveal-gate and multi-hop-escalation scenarios — but the guards live under `test/system`, `test/cluster` and `test/governance`, not a `test/security` folder, and every guarantee is scoped honestly in its doc. What is not present is a single formal threat model tying those guarantees together.

Softanza's security advantage is not a better crypto library — it is a governance doctrine enforced uniformly: one capability lattice under which an LLM cannot act effectfully, a tamper-evident ledger, and a full identity stack, all feeding one CI gate. The gaps that matter are the classic surfaces that doctrine has not yet absorbed — injection defense, data-at-rest sealing, and foreign-code governance.
